abstract.text: Emergency Departments (EDs) see a high prevalence of people who smoke, many of whom present with acute smoking-related conditions (e.g., myocardial infarction, stroke, pneumonia, and asthma/COPD exacerbations). The immediacy of illness creates a strong "teachable moment," increasing receptiveness to risk communication and behavior change. Evidence indicates that pairing brief counseling with point-of-care therapeutic support and structured follow-up improves abstinence, although effects vary with local infrastructure, product availability, and staffing models. Despite this promise, scale-up is often constrained by economic barriers, limited staffing and training, and weak integration of cessation workflows into routine ED practice. The aim of this article is to provide a reality check on ED-based smoking cessation by synthesizing evidence on effectiveness, feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and safety across health-system contexts, and by outlining pragmatic delivery models and research priorities. Embedding low-friction, clinically governed cessation bundles within EDs has the potential to convert acute presentations into durable quit attempts and reduce smoking-related harm at scale, though this population-level impact remains a hypothesis to be tested. Future work should prioritize pragmatic and implementation trials with biochemically verified outcomes, integration metrics, equity impacts, and cost-utility analyses to guide sustainable adoption across diverse settings.

articles.title: The impact of faculty development interventions on supervisor narrative feedback quality in competency-based medical education.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Improving the feedback that supervisors provide trainees in medical education is challenging. The development of automated methods of rating the quality of narrative feedback has created an opportunity to quantify the impact of interventions focused on this goal.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We used a previously developed natural language processing model based on the Quality Assessment of Learning (QuAL) score to rate the quality of each comment in our Royal College Emergency Medicine specialty training program from July 2018 to June 2024. We quantified the effectiveness of three faculty development interventions (e-mail feedback, audit and feedback workshops, and assessment form modifications) by comparing pre- and post-intervention QuAL scores.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: During the study period 9709 narrative comments were scored. The average QuAL score rose from 3.2/5 in 2019 to 4.5/5 in 2024. All interventions resulted in an overall improvement in the mean QuAL score as measured by assessor weighted mean: individual e-mail with suggestions for improvement (35.1%), assessment form template change (24.3%), workshop (19.1%) and individual e-mail thanking them for their high-quality comments (11.0%).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: By combining a multi-faceted faculty development approach with a scalable measurement of our outcome, we have demonstrated an improvement in supervisor narrative comment quality and quantified the impact of each intervention. While it is likely that the interventions were complementary, individual e-mails to faculty with suggestions for improvement and modifications to the assessment form were associated with largest improvements in quality. These results may guide to other programs seeking to improve the quality of supervisor narrative comments.

articles.title: Predictive factors for psychotropic medication prescription in child and adolescent psychiatric emergency care: a machine learning approach using a health data warehouse.

abstract.text: Emergency department (ED) visits for child and adolescent psychiatric presentations have increased in recent years. Psychotropic treatments are frequently used during visit, and sometimes at discharge. However, there are no clear guidelines, and current practices are poorly described and understood in this domain. We propose exploring these practices and the factors leading to psychotropic medication in emergency settings in-visit and at discharge for children and adolescents. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 1,527 patients seen at Necker Hospital (Paris, France) between 2021 and 2025, using clinical data warehouse (CDW) data. Sociodemographic and clinical variables, psychotropic administration during the ED stay, and prescriptions at discharge were analyzed using multilevel logistic regression and gradient boosting models, integrating structured data and SNOMED concepts extracted from free-text notes. Among 2,060 psychiatric ED visits, psychotropic medications were administered in 21.9% and prescribed at discharge in 13.9%. In-ED administration was mainly driven by markers of acute severity, including prolonged length of stay, older age, psychiatric diagnosis, and frequent ED use, while anxiety disorders were associated with lower odds. In contrast, discharge prescriptions were independently associated with in-ED psychotropic administration, psychiatric diagnosis, and socioeconomic context. Models using free text in addition to structured data significantly improved prediction, allowing for a comprehensive and global understanding of factors involved in prescribing. Psychotropic use in pediatric psychiatric emergencies reflects distinct processes of acute symptom management and discharge decision-making, influenced by different clinical and social factors. Leveraging unstructured clinical data enhances understanding of these practices and may inform future guidelines and continuity of care.

articles.title: Triage Administration of Ondansetron for Gastroenteritis in Children: A Randomized Controlled Trial.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: Acute gastroenteritis is a leading cause of pediatric emergency department (ED) visits. While ondansetron reduces vomiting, intravenous rehydration, and hospital admissions, its efficacy when initiated at triage remains unclear. We aimed to evaluate whether triage nurse-initiated administration of ondansetron in children with suspected gastroenteritis reduces the proportion of patients who had observation following initial physician assessment.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in a tertiary pediatric ED in Canada. Children aged 6 months to 17 years presenting with ≥4 episodes of vomiting in the preceding 24 hours (including ≥1 within 2 h of arrival) were eligible. At triage, we randomized participants to receive liquid ondansetron or a color- and taste-matched placebo. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients who had observation after the first physician evaluation. Secondary outcomes included postintervention vomiting, ED length of stay, patient comfort, and 48-hour return visits. The trial was registered at clinicaltrials.gov (NCT03052361).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Recruitment was stopped prematurely due to the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic. Ninety-one participants were randomized to ondansetron (n = 44) or placebo (n = 47). Overall, 40 patients (45%) were discharged immediately after the initial physician assessment, with no difference between the ondansetron and placebo groups (44% vs. 45%; absolute difference: -1%, 95% CI: -20% to 19%). No significant differences were observed in any secondary outcomes.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: This trial failed to show an impact of triage nurse-initiated ondansetron administration in children with presumed gastroenteritis. Although underpowered to assess any outcome, our results could inform researchers planning larger trials.

articles.title: Expert Consensus on the Emergency Treatment of Oral Bleeding.
articles.journal_full: The Chinese journal of dental research
authors: Chinese Stomatological Association Group Standards T
CHSA 098-2025, Society of Oral Emergency, Chinese Stomatological Association

abstract.text: Oral bleeding refers to haemorrhage occurring in the oral and maxillofacial region that does not stop spontaneously, resulting from either local factors, such as inflammation, trauma or tumours, or systemic conditions, such as haematological diseases, severe liver dysfunction or drug-related coagulopathy. Due to the abundant vascular supply in this region, blood loss can be substantial. Moreover, the admixture of blood with saliva often leads patients to mistakenly perceive the haemorrhage as more severe than it is, inducing significant anxiety. Patients with major maxillofacial trauma or systemic coagulation disorders may develop life-threatening complications including airway obstruction and hypovolemic shock. This consensus provides a framework for the emergency management of oral bleeding, encompassing pre-examination triage, principles and protocols for emergency treatment and site-specific recommendations for managing common oral haemorrhages. The aim is to standardise emergency care, assist clinicians in rapidly identifying critical conditions, achieve prompt haemostasis and ultimately improve the safety and efficiency of emergency management for patients with oral bleeding. This document is developed based on a review of the relevant literature and current clinical practices in select medical institutions and may be adapted according to the resources and circumstances of individual health care settings.

articles.title: Age-related patterns in paediatric paracetamol poisoning: a retrospective cohort study, 2015-2025.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Paracetamol poisoning is a common cause of paediatric drug toxicity, but contemporary data on incidence trends, management, and predictors of toxicity remain limited. This study will evaluate incidence trends, clinical features, management, and dose-concentration relationships in paediatric patients with paracetamol poisoning.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Retrospective cohort study of patients aged ≤16 years evaluated at a tertiary hospital (2015-2025). Cases were identified through serum paracetamol measurements and classified by exposure pattern. Acetylcysteine administration was assessed according to TOXBASE-based institutional criteria. Spearman's correlation between reported dose (mg/kg) and serum concentration was analysed in acute overdoses.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 271 cases were included (114 aged ≤9 years; 157 aged 10-16 years). The incidence of identified cases of suspected paediatric paracetamol poisoning increased from 1.11 to 8.68 cases per 10,000 paediatric inhabitants between 2018 and 2025. Adolescents more frequently had intentional overdoses (96.8% versus 0%), higher reported doses (median 212.7 versus 150 mg/kg), and higher serum paracetamol concentrations (median 59.5 versus 30 mg/L [393.9 versus 198.6 µmol/L]) (P < 0.001). Acetylcysteine was administered in 69.2% of cases and was considered inappropriate in 17% of treated patients, predominantly among younger children. Hepatotoxicity (ALT > 3 × ULN and/or bilirubin > 2 × ULN) occurred in 21.4%, and acute liver failure (according to established paediatric criteria) in 9.2%, without significant differences between age groups. In acute overdoses with serum concentrations measured 4-24 h after ingestion, correlation between reported dose and serum concentration was weak in adolescents (ρ = 0.44; P < 0.001) and very weak in younger children (ρ = 0.28; P = 0.04).

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Consistent with previous paediatric toxicology studies, exposure patterns differed by age group, with predominantly accidental exposures in younger children and intentional overdoses in adolescents.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Reported ingested dose showed only weak correlation with serum paracetamol concentrations, particularly in younger children. These findings suggest that exposure history alone is insufficient for poisoning risk assessment and should be interpreted alongside sampling time and biochemical evaluation.

articles.title: Relationship Between Blood Volume Collected and Contamination Rates of Blood Cultures in Paediatric Emergencies: A Study Protocol.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: Blood culture is the gold standard for diagnosing bloodstream infections and guiding antimicrobial therapy. However, the optimal blood volume for paediatric blood cultures remains uncertain. This study evaluated the effectiveness of a standardized paediatric blood culture collection protocol using age- and weight-adjusted blood volumes to reduce contamination rates while maintaining diagnostic performance.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A cross-sectional study will be conducted in the paediatric emergency department of a tertiary hospital. All patients under 18 years of age undergoing blood culture collection were included. Data on blood collection practices, inoculated blood volume, contamination rates and culture positivity will be collected and analysed using STATA version 18.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Implementation of the protocol was expected to reduce blood culture contamination rates without compromising diagnostic yield. The study will assess the feasibility and effectiveness of using lower age- and weight-adjusted blood volumes in routine paediatric emergency care.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: If effective, this protocol may support the adoption of less invasive blood culture collection strategies, improving sample quality, reducing contamination and enhancing the safety and quality of care for paediatric patients.

articles.title: Brodifacoum poisoning complicated by intestinal necrosis.
Establishing the value of call-handling metrics in a United Kingdom Poisons Information Centre.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Poisons Information Centres in the United Kingdom have experienced increased enquiry volume over the past five years, accompanied by declining answer rates, together indicating increasing operational pressure on Specialists in Poisons Information. Accurate measurement of enquiry handling time is essential for understanding workload and informing workforce planning; however, the validity of routinely collected operational metrics has not been evaluated.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We undertook a service evaluation to compare automated timestamps from the national enquiry-logging system with manually recorded handling times. Handling time was defined as the sum of 'talk', 'hold' and 'documentation' time. Data were self-collected across 48 call handling shifts, involving 821 enquiries. For each enquiry, manually recorded handling time was compared with the system-generated duration to assess alignment and, if applicable, to quantify the magnitude and direction of any discrepancy.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Automated timestamps did not provide an accurate measure of total handling time, with bidirectional errors observed across Specialists in Poisons Information irrespective of experience. System-generated durations typically underestimated true handling time by approximately 20%, equating to a cumulative discrepancy of 30-80 min per shift. The median manually determined handling time for an incoming enquiry was 538 s, with 78% of time spent talking to the enquirer and 22% on documentation. Handling times were substantially longer for hospital-originated enquiries (828 s). The median case handling time also increased linearly with increasing case severity.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Growing enquiry volume and reduced answer rates motivated assessment of automated timestamp data, which underestimated true handling time. Wide variability indicated routine metrics may lack validity for describing workload or informing operational decisions.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Automated timestamping substantially underestimates true enquiry handling time and may misrepresent workloads in Poison Information Centres. Accurate measurement of handling time is essential for modelling capacity, determining safe staffing levels and ensuring that national performance targets remain achievable.

articles.title: Developmental Variation in the Association Between Substance Use and Firearm Aggression From Adolescence to Emerging Adulthood: A Time-Varying Effect Modeling Approach.
articles.journal_full: Journal of studies on alcohol and drugs

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Firearm assault injury is a leading cause of death among adolescents and emerging adults. Less is known about how firearm aggression (i.e., using a firearm to threaten or injure someone) varies developmentally during this life stage, and how demographic factors and substance use contribute to its trajectory.

abstract.label: METHOD
abstract.text: Participants were 599 individuals aged 16 to 25 who sought emergency care in Flint, Michigan, and reported past-six-month drug use. An accelerated cohort design was used to organize the data by respondents' age in quarter-year increments at the time of measurement; each participant contributed up to five repeated assessments. Time-varying effect models (TVEM) were used to examine how sociodemographic characteristics and alcohol, cigarette, and cannabis use frequencies were associated with the likelihood of firearm aggression across age.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: The probability of firearm aggression peaked at the onset of emerging adulthood (ages 18-20). Being male was positively associated with firearm aggression during adolescence into emerging adulthood. Alcohol use frequency was also positively associated with firearm aggression in adolescence, with effects diminished by emerging adulthood. Cannabis and cigarette use frequencies, as well as race, parental education, and public assistance, were not associated with firearm aggression across age.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Firearm aggression was most prevalent as youth transitioned into emerging adulthood from adolescence, particularly among males and youth who used alcohol more frequently. This may reflect a period of developmental vulnerability involving ongoing maturation in self-regulation and emerging norms around masculinity, particularly among youth in under-resourced communities where community violence is prevalent.

articles.title: Facilitators and barriers for interdisciplinary collaboration in pediatric palliative care: A cross-sectional survey.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Pediatric palliative care requires input from various healthcare professionals to meet the changing needs of children and their families. Effective interdisciplinary collaboration across care settings is essential to ensure continuity and quality of care.

abstract.label: AIM
abstract.text: To identify facilitators and barriers for interdisciplinary collaboration within pediatric palliative care as perceived by diverse healthcare professionals.

abstract.label: DESIGN
abstract.text: Cross-sectional survey in which participants reflected on their most recent pediatric palliative care case, using the Index of Interdisciplinary Collaboration, and reported their satisfaction with care coordination, continuity, and quality in this case.

abstract.label: SETTING/PARTICIPANTS
abstract.text: Physicians, nurses, and paramedical professionals in home care, regional, and academic hospitals who had provided palliative care within the previous 3 years. As pediatric palliative care may extend over a longer period, participants reflected on collaboration during the entire care process for a now-deceased child.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: In total, 208 healthcare professionals participated. Fifteen facilitators and six barriers were identified. Facilitators included role clarity, task flexibility, family participation, and the perceived importance and added value of interdisciplinary collaboration and included active collaboration with home care nurses, Children's Palliative Care Teams and lead clinicians. Barriers related mainly to insufficient communication, limited evaluation, and inadequate organization of interdisciplinary collaboration. Satisfaction with care coordination, continuity and quality was high.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Improving interdisciplinary collaboration in pediatric palliative care requires strategies that strengthen organizational and managerial structures, while actively engaging both experienced and less experienced professionals across different care settings. Enhancing awareness of each other's roles, needs, and capacities is essential to foster more effective interdisciplinary collaboration.

articles.title: Focused transthoracic echocardiography in acute pulmonary embolism: a systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy.
articles.journal_full: European journal of emergency medicine : official journal of the European Society for Emergency Medicine

abstract.text: Computed tomography pulmonary angiography is the diagnostic gold standard for acute pulmonary embolism, but delays and radiation risks necessitate rapid bedside alternatives. To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of isolated point-of-care focused echocardiography and a combined approach of focused echocardiography and lower limb deep vein ultrasound for suspected acute pulmonary embolism. Systematic review and meta-analysis. Adult patients presenting to acute healthcare settings with suspected acute pulmonary embolism. Specific morphological signs [dilated right ventricle (RV), tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion] and highly specific functional signs [McConnell's sign, the 60/60 sign, abnormal interventricular motion, RV outflow tract early systolic notching (ESN), and clot-in-transit] assessed via isolated focused echocardiography, alongside a combined echocardiography and deep vein ultrasound strategy. Bivariate random-effects meta-analysis to determine pooled sensitivity and specificity. Thirty-three studies (3981 patients) were included. Isolated focused echocardiography signs demonstrated poor sensitivities (0.03-0.65) but high specificities, including McConnell's sign (0.98), the 60/60 sign (0.93), and RV outflow tract ESN (0.98). The combined echocardiography and deep vein ultrasound approach yielded a pooled sensitivity of 0.62 and a pooled specificity of 0.98. In this meta-analysis, isolated focused echocardiography signs demonstrated a reportedly low sensitivity but high specificity for the diagnosis of acute pulmonary embolism. Integrating lower limb deep vein ultrasound improves diagnostic sensitivity, though definitive exclusion still requires computed tomography.

articles.title: Defining the "Critical Casualty" through Reference-Standard Constructs, Reporting Completeness, and Reproducibility in Mass-Casualty Incident Triage Research: Methodology Scoping Review.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION/STUDY OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: Mass-casualty incident (MCI) triage algorithms are evaluated against reference standards that operationally define the "critical casualty," yet the constructs underlying these standards and the completeness of their reporting have not been systematically characterized.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A PRISMA-ScR methodology scoping review was conducted using a pre-registered Open Science Framework (OSF) protocol; MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and CINAHL were searched on May 5, 2026 for English-language full-text sources that described, derived, validated, or applied a reference standard for distinguishing critical from non-critical casualties in MCI triage. Reference standards were classified using a pre-specified taxonomy, and reporting completeness was assessed with the eight-item Reference Standard Reporting Index for MCI Triage (RSRI-MCI), developed a priori for this review and not externally validated. Two reviewers independently classified and coded all sources.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Sixty sources published from 2001 through 2025 were included. Operationalized reference standards clustered around four foundational methodological sources, while only five sources (8%) analyzed retrospective data from actual MCIs. Five reference-standard families were identified: Life-Saving Intervention (LSI)-Based (38%), Composite/Hybrid (30%), Expert Panel (15%), Outcome/Resource (12%), and Anatomic Severity (5%); LSI-Based and Composite constructs together accounted for approximately two-thirds of the field. Reporting was asymmetric: definition (98%), components (97%), and rationale (88%) were reported almost universally, whereas time window (40%), dead/expectant handling (57%), binary mapping (65%), missing-data handling (58%), and reference-standard limitations (58%) were reported less consistently. Inter-rater agreement was substantial overall (83%) and for family classification (93%; Gwet's Chance-Corrected Agreement Coefficient [AC1] = 0.919; 95% CI, 0.837-0.980).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Mass-casualty incident triage studies routinely report what their reference standard is but inconsistently report how it is operationalized, particularly its time window. Five reporting recommendations are proposed for future MCI triage validation research.

articles.title: Hurricane-Resilient Electronic Medical Records: A Distributed Architecture for Small Island Developing States.
articles.journal_full: Disaster medicine and public health preparedness

abstract.text: Hurricane Dorian (2019, GLIDE TC-2019-000099-BHS) permanently destroyed decades of patient records in Grand Bahama, The Bahamas, exposing critical vulnerabilities in centralized health care information systems. This study proposes a distributed electronic medical record (EMR) architecture to maintain patient data availability during and after catastrophic hurricanes in small island states. The architecture connects The Bahamas' approximately 75 community health facilities through regional replication hubs, each maintaining a full local database replica with bidirectional synchronization, enabling autonomous operation when facilities are isolated. An external off-island backup site adds resilience against region-wide events, though site selection must weigh correlated hurricane risk. Critical information, including active medications and allergies, receives priority synchronization under bandwidth-limited conditions. Cost projections indicate feasibility for resource-constrained settings ($2.00 per capita capital cost; $0.59 per capita annual operating cost). Governmental support, including national patient identification infrastructure, would strengthen implementation. This proposed framework awaits pilot implementation and has not been deployed operationally.

articles.title: Nursing Workforce Preparedness for Nuclear Emergencies in Japan: A National Facility-Level Survey of Nuclear Emergency Core Hospitals.
articles.journal_full: Disaster medicine and public health preparedness

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: To describe nursing workforce arrangements, training exposure, educational needs, and support needs for nuclear emergency medical care among Nuclear Emergency Core Hospitals (NECHs) in Japan.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This facility-level cross-sectional survey targeted all 51 NECHs. Questionnaire items were developed and reviewed for content validity through internal consensus by 3 study-team nurses or public health nurses; no pilot testing or recruitment reminders were conducted. Facility proportions included exact Clopper-Pearson 95% confidence intervals, and free-text responses underwent qualitative content analysis.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Twenty-two facilities responded (43.1%; exact 95% CI, 29.3-57.8%). Emergency departments (19/22, 86.4%) and DMAT membership (20/22, 90.9%) were common, while certified nurse specialists in radiation nursing were reported by 5 facilities (22.7%). Radiation basics and PPE donning/doffing practice were each selected by 21 facilities (95.5%). Free-text responses yielded 43 meaning units across 5 categories emphasizing recurrent training, workforce maintenance, organizational and financial support, and clearer staffing standards.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Among responding NECHs, nuclear emergency nursing preparedness relied heavily on emergency/disaster nursing infrastructure, while radiation-specific advanced nursing expertise was reported less frequently. Sustainable preparedness may benefit from recurrent practical training, broader access to radiation nursing expertise, organizational support, and policy-level staffing discussion.

articles.title: Social Capital and Disaster Preparedness of Farmers in Severe Earthquake Areas: The Mediating Role of Risk Perception.
articles.journal_full: Disaster medicine and public health preparedness

abstract.text: Improving household disaster preparedness is one of the most effective ways to reduce disaster risk. Based on a survey of 327 farmers in the areas worst hit by the Wenchuan and Ya'an earthquakes, this study systematically analyzed the impact of social capital on disaster preparedness, and the specific mechanism of action between the two was further analyzed using the intermediary effect model. The results show that (1) faced with the threat of earthquake disasters, farmers are not sufficiently prepared to avoid disasters, with only about 25% having made preparations. Farmers' social capital ability is weak, and the scores of farmers' perception of possibility and severity are 47.44 and 67.19, respectively. (2) Farmers' social capital is positively correlated with their disaster preparedness. With other conditions remaining unchanged, the possibility of farmers' disaster preparedness increases by 3.519, 1.050, and 0.766 units for each additional unit of social network, social support, and social participation, respectively. (3) Possibility perception has a partial mediating effect between social capital and disaster avoidance preparedness. Specifically, social participation indirectly affects farmers' disaster preparedness through the possibility perception. Policymakers should consider enhancing farmers' disaster preparedness through social participation.

articles.title: Sudan's Silent Mental Health Crisis: A Systemic Failure of Humanitarian Response.
articles.journal_full: Disaster medicine and public health preparedness

abstract.text: The ongoing conflict in Sudan, which began in April 2023, has triggered a severe but under-recognized mental health crisis. Nearly two-thirds of hospitals in conflict-affected regions are non-functional, supply chains have collapsed, and fewer than 100 psychiatrists serve a population of 45 million. Emerging evidence documents rates of post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, and anxiety among displaced and non-displaced civilians, children, and health workers, yet mental health remains systematically neglected in humanitarian response. This commentary examines the gap between global commitments-including the Sustainable Development Goals and WHO's Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP)-and the realities of care in conflict settings. Drawing on lessons from Syria, Yemen, and Ukraine, we outline a 6-priority framework for immediate mental health integration: (1) training lay health workers for task-shifted psychological support; (2) rebuilding essential psychiatric infrastructure; (3) establishing protected humanitarian corridors for psychotropic medications; (4) expanding tele-psychiatry and remote counselling; (5) integrating mental health into primary and emergency care; and (6) addressing stigma through community engagement. We argue that without explicit funding allocations and operational mandates for mental health services, post-conflict recovery and peacebuilding in Sudan will remain compromised. We call on donors to allocate at least 10% of health-related humanitarian aid to mental health initiatives and for WHO and UNICEF to embed mhGAP in all emergency responses. Sudan represents both an urgent crisis and a global warning: mental health can no longer remain the invisible dimension of humanitarian emergencies.

articles.title: The Relationship Between Trauma Level, Anxiety, Stress, and Coping of Earthquake-Stricken University Students.
articles.journal_full: Disaster medicine and public health preparedness

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: This study aimed to examine the relationships between post-earthquake trauma, anxiety, stress, and stress coping strategies among university students who survived the Kahramanmaraş earthquakes.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This cross-sectional study included 384 university students who survived the Kahramanmaraş earthquakes. Data were collected using a personal information form and standardized scales assessing post-earthquake trauma, anxiety, stress, and stress coping strategies. Descriptive statistics, group comparisons, and correlation analyses were performed.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among the participants, 35.7% had lost a relative, 47.8% had lost a friend, 10.0% reported that their homes were destroyed, 54.0% reported home damage, and 3.1% had been trapped under rubble. A strong positive correlation was found between post-earthquake trauma and anxiety scores (r = 0.714). Participants who had lost a family member, relative, or friend had significantly higher trauma and anxiety scores than those who had not. Trauma scores were also significantly higher among those who were injured, trapped under rubble, or involved in rescue efforts. Significant relationships were found between post-earthquake trauma, anxiety, stress, and stress coping strategies.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Earthquake-related experiences were associated with increased trauma, anxiety, and stress and with stress coping strategies. Early psychological assessment and psychosocial support may help reduce the psychological effects of earthquakes on university students.

articles.title: Clinical and Laboratory Findings When Pediatric Male Sexual Assault Survivors Present to the Emergency Department.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVE
abstract.text: The child sexual abuse (CSA) literature demonstrates that the majority of female pediatric survivors present with normal, uninjured, and uninfected anogenital examinations, yet the clinical presentation of male survivors remains underexplored. This study describes the history, clinical presentation, and medical examination findings of boys and male adolescents presenting to a large urban children's hospital emergency department (ED) seeking care for sexual assault.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A retrospective cross-sectional chart review was conducted for male patients aged 0-18 years who presented to an urban pediatric ED following a chief complaint of CSA or acute sexual assault between October 2019 and March 2024. Data extracted included patient demographics, history of the present illness, elapsed time to evaluation, and documented anogenital examination and laboratory findings.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 92 male patients with 93 system encounters met the inclusion criteria. The median age at presentation was 12.9 years. Like patterns for female counterparts, male sexual abuse survivors evaluated in the ED manifested only rare physical trauma or acute infection. Normal healthy anatomy was documented in 93% of patients who allowed physical examinations. Acute physical injury or positive laboratory findings were identified in only 7% and 3% of tested cases, respectively.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Male pediatric CSA survivors evaluated in the ED rarely manifest anogenital trauma or acute infection upon medical examination. These findings align closely with established female pediatric cohorts and emphasize that a lack of physical or laboratory findings should be anticipated in both male and female pediatric patients disclosing sexual abuse in an acute care setting.
